[Definition 11.1 — Preferences and the Bradley–Terry model]{.tag} Preference data are triples $(x, y_w, y_l)$: for prompt $x$, response $y_w$ was preferred to $y_l$. The Bradley–Terry model (1952) assumes a reward $r$ with
$$
P(y_w \succ y_l \mid x) = \sigma\big(r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l)\big).
$$
A reward model $r_\phi$, a language model with a scalar head, is fitted by maximum likelihood:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RM}}(\phi) = -\mathbb{E} \log \sigma\big(r_\phi(x, y_w) - r_\phi(x, y_l)\big).
$$
:::

::: def
[Definition 11.2 — The KL-regularized objective]{.tag} Starting from a reference policy $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ (the instruction-tuned model), post-training seeks
$$
\max_{\pi}\ \mathbb{E}_{x}\Big[\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi(\cdot \mid x)}\, r(x, y) - \beta\, \mathrm{KL}\big(\pi(\cdot \mid x) \,\|\, \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot \mid x)\big)\Big].
$$
The divergence keeps the policy where the reward model was trained and is reliable; $\beta$ sets the trade-off.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 11.3 — The optimal policy is a tilted reference]{.tag} For each prompt, the objective of Definition 11.2 is maximised by
$$
\pi^*(y \mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)}\, \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)\, \exp\big(r(x, y) / \beta\big).
$$

::: proof
Fix $x$ and write the objective as
$$
J(\pi) = \sum_y \pi(y) \big[r(y) - \beta \log (\pi(y) / \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y))\big].
$$
Since $r = \beta \log (\pi^* Z / \pi_{\mathrm{ref}})$,
$$
J(\pi) = -\beta \sum_y \pi(y) \log \frac{\pi(y)}{\pi^*(y)} + \beta \log Z = -\beta\, \mathrm{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \pi^*) + \beta \log Z,
$$
which is maximal exactly when $\pi = \pi^*$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 11.4 — RLHF with PPO]{.tag} InstructGPT (Ouyang and coauthors, 2022), following Christiano and coauthors (2017), samples responses from the policy, scores them with $r_\phi$ minus a per-token KL penalty, and updates the policy by PPO (Schulman and coauthors, 2017). States are the prompt plus the tokens so far, actions are next tokens, and advantages $A_t$ come from a value network. With the probability ratio $\rho_t$, PPO maximises
$$
\rho_t = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(a_t \mid s_t)}, \qquad L^{\mathrm{CLIP}} = \mathbb{E}_t \big[\min\big(\rho_t A_t,\ \mathrm{clip}(\rho_t, 1 - \epsilon, 1 + \epsilon)\, A_t\big)\big], \qquad \epsilon \approx 0.2.
$$
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 11.5 — What clipping does]{.tag} If $A_t > 0$, the surrogate is constant in $\rho_t$ beyond $1 + \epsilon$; if $A_t < 0$, it is constant below $1 - \epsilon$. In both cases the gradient vanishes there, so one update has no incentive to move the policy far from the one that sampled the data. Proof: compare the two terms of the minimum in each case.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 11.6 — Direct preference optimization (Rafailov and coauthors, 2023)]{.tag} Inverting Theorem 11.3 writes the reward through the optimal policy:
$$
r(x, y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)} + \beta \log Z(x).
$$
In the Bradley–Terry model the term $\log Z(x)$ cancels, which suggests fitting the policy directly:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta) = -\mathbb{E} \log \sigma\Big(\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w \mid x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l \mid x)}\Big).
$$
If preferences follow the Bradley–Terry model with reward $r$ and cover all pairs of responses, the minimiser over policies is $\pi^*$.

::: proof
The DPO loss is the reward-model loss of Definition 11.1 for the implicit reward
$$
\hat r_\theta(x, y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)}.
$$
Every reward equals such an implicit reward up to a function of $x$, which cancels in the loss, so minimising over policies is minimising over rewards. With full coverage, the maximum-likelihood reward is the true $r$ up to a function of $x$. Theorem 11.3 then identifies the policy as $\pi^*$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 11.7 — The DPO gradient]{.tag} With $\hat r_\theta$ as above,
$$
\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}} = -\beta\, \mathbb{E}\Big[\sigma\big(\hat r_\theta(y_l) - \hat r_\theta(y_w)\big) \big(\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y_w \mid x) - \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)\big)\Big].
$$
It raises the preferred response and lowers the other, more strongly when the implicit reward orders them wrongly. Proof: the derivative of $-\log \sigma(z)$ is $-\sigma(-z)$.
:::

::: ex
[Example 11.8 — DPO recovers the tilted policy]{.tag} One prompt, five candidate answers, preferences drawn from a Bradley–Terry model.

```python
import torch
torch.manual_seed(0); torch.set_num_threads(1)

K, beta = 5, 0.5
r_true = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.5, 0.0, -0.5, -1.0])               # hidden rewards
log_ref = torch.log(torch.tensor([0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.2, 0.1]))     # reference policy

i, j = torch.randint(K, (20000,)), torch.randint(K, (20000,))
keep = i != j
i, j = i[keep], j[keep]
i_wins = torch.rand(len(i)) < torch.sigmoid(r_true[i] - r_true[j])
yw, yl = torch.where(i_wins, i, j), torch.where(i_wins, j, i)

logits = log_ref.clone().requires_grad_(True)                     # start at the reference
opt = torch.optim.Adam([logits], lr=0.05)
for step in range(500):
    logp = torch.log_softmax(logits, 0)
    margin = beta * ((logp[yw] - log_ref[yw]) - (logp[yl] - log_ref[yl]))
    loss = -torch.nn.functional.logsigmoid(margin).mean()        # DPO loss
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

print("DPO policy:     ", [round(p, 3) for p in torch.softmax(logits, 0).tolist()])
print("closed form pi*:", [round(p, 3) for p in torch.softmax(log_ref + r_true / beta, 0).tolist()])
```

The two lines agree to about 0.01: $(0.409, 0.302, 0.239, 0.042, 0.008)$ against $(0.418, 0.307, 0.226, 0.042, 0.008)$. No reward model and no sampling were needed.
:::

::: note
[Remark 11.9 — AI feedback and over-optimisation]{.tag} RLAIF replaces human labels by preferences produced by a model; Constitutional AI (Bai and coauthors, 2022) guides that model with a list of written principles. A reward model is only a proxy: optimising it too hard eventually lowers the true quality (Gao, Schulman and Hilton, 2023), which the KL term and early stopping limit.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 11

-   Preferences are modelled by Bradley–Terry; a reward model is fitted by logistic loss on pairs.
-   The KL-regularized objective has a closed-form optimum, the reference tilted by $\exp(r/\beta)$ (Theorem 11.3).
-   PPO optimises it by sampling, with a clipped surrogate; DPO fits it directly by a logistic loss on log-ratio differences (Theorem 11.6).
:::

## 12. Retrieval-augmented and graph-augmented generation {#ch12}

The knowledge of a language model is frozen in its weights at the end of pretraining, cannot be cited, and is sometimes reconstructed wrongly when it is missing. Retrieval-augmented generation fetches evidence at query time and conditions the answer on it; graph-augmented generation fetches structured evidence that supports multi-step reasoning.

::: def
[Definition 12.1 — BM25]{.tag} The standard sparse retrieval score (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009) of a document $d$ for a query $q$ is, with the non-negative idf of common implementations,
$$
\mathrm{BM25}(q, d) = \sum_{t \in q} \mathrm{idf}(t)\, \frac{\mathrm{tf}(t, d)\, (k_1 + 1)}{\mathrm{tf}(t, d) + k_1 \big(1 - b + b\, |d| / \mathrm{avdl}\big)}, \qquad \mathrm{idf}(t) = \log\Big(1 + \frac{N - \mathrm{df}(t) + 0.5}{\mathrm{df}(t) + 0.5}\Big),
$$
with $k_1 \in [1.2, 2]$ and $b = 0.75$ as usual values. Repeated terms saturate at $k_1 + 1$, and long documents are penalised.
:::

::: def
[Definition 12.2 — Dense passage retrieval (Karpukhin and coauthors, 2020)]{.tag} Two encoders map questions and passages to vectors, and the score is their inner product $s(q, p) = E_Q(q)^\top E_P(p)$. On a batch of $B$ question–passage pairs, the other passages of the batch serve as negatives:
$$
\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^{B} \log \frac{\exp s(q_i, p_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{B} \exp s(q_i, p_j)}.
$$
This is a $B$-way softmax classification (Proposition 0.2) with $B - 1$ negatives for free. Passages are encoded offline, and retrieval is an approximate maximum inner-product search, for example with FAISS (Johnson, Douze and Jégou, 2019).
:::

::: def
[Definition 12.3 — Retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis and coauthors, 2020)]{.tag} A retriever gives a distribution $p_\eta(z \mid x)$ over the top-$K$ passages and a generator models $p_\theta(y \mid x, z)$. RAG-sequence marginalises over passages:
$$
p(y \mid x) \approx \sum_{z \in \text{top-}K} p_\eta(z \mid x) \prod_t p_\theta(y_t \mid x, z, y_{<t}).
$$
With today's large language models, the retrieved passages are usually placed in the prompt, and only the retriever is trained or tuned.
:::

::: note
[Remark 12.4 — Grounding and hallucination]{.tag} A hallucination is fluent content that is not supported by the source or by facts (survey by Ji and coauthors, 2023). Retrieval reduces it when the answer is asked to rely on the retrieved passages, to cite them, and to abstain when retrieval scores are low; claims can then be checked against the evidence.

Retrieval quality (recall at $k$, mean reciprocal rank) and faithfulness of the answer should be measured separately. Long contexts are no full substitute: Liu and coauthors (2024) find that models use information placed in the middle of a long context less well.
:::

::: def
[Definition 12.5 — Knowledge graphs and multi-hop questions]{.tag} A knowledge graph is a set of triples $(h, r, t)$: head entity, relation, tail entity. A multi-hop question needs a chain of triples. A passage retriever scores each passage against the question separately, so it finds the first hop and misses the next ones, whose passages share no words with the question.
:::

::: def
[Definition 12.6 — Message passing and graph-augmented pipelines]{.tag} A message-passing layer (Gilmer and coauthors, 2017) updates each node from its neighbours:
$$
h_v^{(\ell + 1)} = \phi\Big(h_v^{(\ell)}, \sum_{u \in \mathcal{N}(v)} \psi\big(h_u^{(\ell)}, h_v^{(\ell)}, e_{uv}\big)\Big).
$$
A graph-augmented LLM links the entities of the question to the graph and retrieves a subgraph: a $k$-hop neighbourhood, paths, or a relevant connected subgraph. G-Retriever (He and coauthors, 2024) selects it as a prize-collecting Steiner tree. The subgraph reaches the LLM as verbalised triples, or as a soft prompt computed by message passing.
:::

::: ex
[Example 12.7 — Where BM25 stops and the graph continues]{.tag}

```python
import math, re
from collections import Counter
import networkx as nx

docs = ["BARThez is a French sequence-to-sequence model pretrained like BART.",
        "BART was introduced by Lewis and coauthors at Facebook AI.",
        "FrugalScore distils expensive evaluation metrics into small models.",
        "The k-core of a graph of words keeps its densest terms.",
        "Facebook AI Research has a laboratory in Paris."]
tok = lambda s: re.findall(r"[a-z0-9\-]+", s.lower())
D = [tok(d) for d in docs]
avgdl, N = sum(map(len, D)) / len(D), len(D)
df = Counter(t for d in D for t in set(d))

def bm25(query, k1=1.5, b=0.75):
    scores = []
    for d in D:
        tf, s = Counter(d), 0.0
        for t in tok(query):
            if t in tf:
                idf = math.log(1 + (N - df[t] + 0.5) / (df[t] + 0.5))
                s += idf * tf[t] * (k1 + 1) / (tf[t] + k1 * (1 - b + b * len(d) / avgdl))
        scores.append(s)
    return sorted(range(N), key=lambda i: -scores[i])

q = "In which city does the lab behind the model that BARThez imitates work?"
print("BM25 top-2:", bm25(q)[:2])            # [0, 3]: first hop only

KG = nx.DiGraph()                            # triples extracted from the documents
for h, r, t in [("BARThez", "pretrained_like", "BART"), ("BART", "introduced_by", "Facebook AI"),
                ("Facebook AI", "has_lab_in", "Paris"), ("FrugalScore", "distils", "metrics")]:
    KG.add_edge(h, t, rel=r)
linked = [e for e in KG if e.lower() in q.lower()]          # naive entity linking
sub = nx.compose_all([nx.ego_graph(KG, e, radius=3) for e in linked])
context = [f"{u} {KG[u][v]['rel']} {v}." for u, v in nx.bfs_edges(sub, linked[0])]
print("graph context for the LLM:", " ".join(context))
```

BM25 returns the BARThez document and an irrelevant one; the 3-hop subgraph around the linked entity contains the whole chain BARThez → BART → Facebook AI → Paris.
:::

::: note
[Remark 12.8 — GraphRAG and relational databases]{.tag} GraphRAG (Edge and coauthors, 2024) builds the graph from the corpus itself. An LLM extracts entities and relations, Leiden community detection (Traag, Waltman and van Eck, 2019) groups them, the LLM summarises each community, and a global question is answered by combining the summaries. It targets questions about a whole corpus that no single passage answers.

For relational databases, the LLM writes an SQL query from the question and the schema (text-to-SQL); running it returns exact evidence that can be checked.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 12

-   BM25 and dense dual encoders retrieve passages; dense retrievers are trained with in-batch negatives.
-   RAG conditions generation on retrieved evidence, which allows citations and reduces hallucination; retrieval and faithfulness are evaluated separately.
-   Graph augmentation retrieves chains of triples, verbalised or encoded by message passing; GraphRAG summarises communities of an extracted graph; text-to-SQL queries databases.
:::

## 13. Quantization and efficient inference {#ch13}

A 7-billion-parameter model stored in 16-bit floats needs 14 GB for its weights alone, and decoding reads all of them for every generated token. Quantization stores weights, and sometimes activations, on 8 or 4 bits; the key–value cache and pruning address the other costs of inference.

::: def
[Definition 13.1 — Uniform quantization]{.tag} With $b$ bits and $q_{\max} = 2^{b-1} - 1$, symmetric absmax quantization of a group of weights $w$ uses the scale $s = \max_i |w_i| / q_{\max}$ and
$$
Q(w) = s \cdot \mathrm{clamp}\big(\mathrm{round}(w / s),\, -q_{\max},\, q_{\max}\big).
$$
The scale is stored in 16 bits per tensor, per output channel, or per group of $g$ consecutive weights ($g = 64$ or $128$ are common). Asymmetric schemes add a zero point.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 13.2 — Rounding error and outliers]{.tag} Every weight satisfies $|Q(w_i) - w_i| \leq s/2$, and if rounding errors are uniformly spread the mean squared error is $s^2 / 12$. Since $s$ is proportional to the largest weight of the group, one outlier enlarges the error of every weight that shares its scale. Small groups contain outliers, at a storage cost of
$$
b + 16 / g \ \text{bits per weight}, \qquad \text{for example } 4.125 \text{ bits for } b = 4,\ g = 128.
$$
:::

::: def
[Definition 13.3 — LLM.int8(), NF4 and bitsandbytes]{.tag} Dettmers and coauthors (2022) observe that, beyond a few billion parameters, a few hidden dimensions carry activations of very large magnitude. LLM.int8() multiplies matrices in 8 bits with vector-wise scales, and computes these outlier dimensions in 16 bits.

NF4 (QLoRA, Dettmers and coauthors, 2023) places its 16 levels at quantiles of a standard normal law, which suits normally distributed weights, and also quantizes the scales. QLoRA trains LoRA adapters (ch. 10) on a frozen 4-bit model. Both are implemented in the bitsandbytes library.
:::

::: def
[Definition 13.4 — Layer-wise post-training quantization]{.tag} Given calibration inputs $X \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times n}$ of a linear layer $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$, find a quantized $\hat W$ minimising the output error:
$$
\min_{\hat W} \|W X - \hat W X\|_F^2.
$$
Rows are independent. For one row, a change $\delta$ costs $\frac12 \delta^\top H \delta$ with Hessian $H = 2 X X^\top$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 13.5 — Optimal compensation (Hassibi and Stork, 1993; Frantar and coauthors, 2023)]{.tag} Fix coordinate $q$ of a row $w$ to its quantized value. The other coordinates are best updated by $\delta$, and the error then grows by $\Delta E$:
$$
\delta = -\frac{w_q - Q(w_q)}{[H^{-1}]_{qq}}\, H^{-1} e_q, \qquad \Delta E = \frac{\big(w_q - Q(w_q)\big)^2}{2\, [H^{-1}]_{qq}}.
$$

::: proof
Minimise $\frac12 \delta^\top H \delta$ under the constraint $e_q^\top \delta = Q(w_q) - w_q$. The Lagrange condition $H \delta = \lambda e_q$ gives $\delta = \lambda H^{-1} e_q$. The constraint gives $\lambda = (Q(w_q) - w_q) / [H^{-1}]_{qq}$, and the cost is $\frac12 \lambda^2 [H^{-1}]_{qq}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

GPTQ quantizes the columns in a fixed order shared by all rows, applies this update to the columns not yet quantized, and removes column $q$ from $H^{-1}$ by Gaussian elimination. With lazy batched updates and a Cholesky form, the authors quantize 175-billion-parameter models in about four GPU hours.
::::

::: def
[Definition 13.6 — Activation-aware weight quantization, AWQ (Lin and coauthors, 2024)]{.tag} A small fraction of weight channels matters most, and it is identified by the magnitude of the activations, not of the weights. Rather than keep them in 16 bits, AWQ scales input channel $j$ by $s_j > 1$ before quantizing and divides the activation:
$$
y = Q\big(W\, \mathrm{diag}(s)\big)\, \mathrm{diag}(s)^{-1} x.
$$
If the group scale is unchanged, the rounding error carried by channel $j$ is divided by $s_j$. AWQ sets $s_j = \bar{x}_j^{\,\alpha}$ from the mean activation magnitude, with $\alpha \in [0, 1]$ chosen on calibration data, without back-propagation.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 13.7 — Size of the KV cache]{.tag} Decoding stores the keys and values of all past tokens, for every layer and key–value head:
$$
\text{memory} = 2 \times n_{\text{layers}} \times n_{\text{kv heads}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times T \times \text{batch} \times \text{bytes}.
$$
With 32 layers, 32 heads of dimension 128 and 16-bit values, that is 0.5 MiB per token, or 2 GiB for one sequence of 4096 tokens.

Multi-query attention (Shazeer, 2019) and grouped-query attention (Ainslie and coauthors, 2023) share key–value heads and divide this memory. PagedAttention (Kwon and coauthors, 2023) allocates it in blocks to avoid fragmentation, and the cache itself can be quantized.
:::

::: ex
[Example 13.8 — Round-to-nearest versus GPTQ]{.tag} A layer with two outlier input channels and strongly correlated calibration inputs, quantized on 4 bits.

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def quant(w, scale, bits=4):
    qmax = 2 ** (bits - 1) - 1
    return scale * np.clip(np.round(w / scale), -qmax, qmax)

d_in, d_out, n = 128, 64, 2048
W = rng.normal(size=(d_out, d_in)) / np.sqrt(d_in)
W[:, :2] *= 8                                              # two outlier input channels
mix = rng.normal(size=(d_in, d_in)) * np.logspace(0, -2, d_in)
X = mix @ rng.normal(size=(d_in, n))                       # correlated calibration inputs
err = lambda Wq: np.linalg.norm((W - Wq) @ X) ** 2 / np.linalg.norm(W @ X) ** 2

def scales(W, group):                                      # one scale per row and group
    s = np.abs(W.reshape(len(W), -1, group)).max(axis=2) / 7
    return np.repeat(s, group, axis=1)

def gptq(W, X, S, damp=0.01):
    W = W.copy()
    H = 2 * X @ X.T
    H += damp * np.mean(np.diag(H)) * np.eye(len(H))       # dampening
    Hinv = np.linalg.inv(H)
    for q in range(W.shape[1]):
        wq = quant(W[:, q], S[:, q])
        e = (W[:, q] - wq) / Hinv[q, q]
        W[:, q:] -= np.outer(e, Hinv[q, q:])               # Theorem 13.5
        W[:, q] = wq
        Hinv -= np.outer(Hinv[:, q], Hinv[q, :]) / Hinv[q, q]   # eliminate column q
    return W

for group in [d_in, 32]:
    S = scales(W, group)
    print(f"group size {group:3d}: RTN error {err(quant(W, S)):.4f}, "
          f"GPTQ error {err(gptq(W, X, S)):.4f}")
```

Per-row scales give a relative output error of 0.076 for round-to-nearest and 0.013 for GPTQ; groups of 32 give 0.020 and 0.001. Smaller groups (Proposition 13.2) and error compensation (Theorem 13.5) each help, and they combine.
:::

::: note
[Remark 13.9 — Pruning]{.tag} Magnitude pruning removes the smallest weights. Wanda (Sun and coauthors, 2024) scores a weight by its magnitude times the norm of its input activation, and SparseGPT (Frantar and Alistarh, 2023) applies the compensation of Theorem 13.5 to removed weights. The 2:4 pattern, two zeros in every group of four weights, is accelerated by recent GPUs; unstructured sparsity saves memory but rarely time.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 13

-   Uniform quantization has error at most half a step; outliers inflate the step of their whole group.
-   LLM.int8() isolates outlier dimensions, NF4 matches normal weights, GPTQ compensates rounding errors with the inverse Hessian, AWQ rescales salient channels.
-   The KV cache grows linearly with context and batch; sharing key–value heads and paging control it.
:::

## 14. Research directions and open problems {#ch14}

This chapter is for self-study. It points to active questions that extend each part of the course, with entry papers; it is a map, not a survey.

::: note
[Remark 14.1 — Graphs and text, beyond bags of words]{.tag} Graph-of-words methods (ch. 3) keep finding uses where data are scarce and interpretability matters. Work by Shang and coauthors (2018) builds word graphs of meeting transcripts and compresses them into abstractive summaries without supervision; message passing on graphs-of-words (Nikolentzos, Tixier and Vazirgiannis, 2020) brings the same structure into neural classifiers.

Open questions: how to combine degeneracy-based scores with contextual embeddings, and whether graph-based keyword extraction still adds value as a retrieval signal for RAG pipelines (ch. 12).
:::

::: note
[Remark 14.2 — Long contexts and efficient attention]{.tag} The quadratic cost of attention (Definition 6.5) drives two lines of work. FlashAttention (Dao and coauthors, 2022) computes exact attention in tiles that stay in fast GPU memory, cutting memory traffic. Selective state-space models such as Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023) replace attention by a recurrence with input-dependent parameters, linear in the length — a return of the RNNs of ch. 4 in a parallelisable form. Whether such models match Transformers on retrieval-heavy tasks, and how positional schemes such as RoPE and ALiBi extrapolate far beyond the training length, are open.
:::

::: note
[Remark 14.3 — Alignment, reasoning and their theory]{.tag} DPO (Theorem 11.6) assumes the Bradley–Terry model; Azar and coauthors (2024) show that it can overfit when preferences are nearly deterministic and propose a regularised variant (IPO). Reward over-optimisation (Gao, Schulman and Hilton, 2023) remains poorly understood.

Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards — checking a final answer in mathematics or code — has become central to training models that reason step by step; GRPO (Shao and coauthors, 2024) removes the value network of PPO by normalising rewards within a group of samples. What these methods teach, beyond eliciting abilities already present after pretraining, is debated.
:::

::: note
[Remark 14.4 — Evaluation that keeps up]{.tag} Benchmarks saturate and leak into pretraining corpora. LLM-as-a-judge evaluation (Zheng and coauthors, 2023) scales human-like judgements but inherits position and verbosity biases; learned metrics such as FrugalScore (ch. 9) raise the same question of what exactly is distilled. Open problems: contamination detection without access to the training data, error bars for judge-based scores (Proposition 9.9), and native-sourced benchmarks for the many languages that still have none.
:::

::: note
[Remark 14.5 — Multilingual and sovereign models]{.tag} Tokenizers trained mostly on English penalise other languages in cost and context length (Petrov and coauthors, 2023; Rust and coauthors, 2021). Research asks how much a dedicated tokenizer, continued pretraining (Remark 9.10) or vocabulary transfer recovers, how to evaluate cultural knowledge rather than translated knowledge, and how small, well-trained regional models compare with large multilingual ones under the compute accounting of ch. 8.
:::

::: note
[Remark 14.6 — Graphs and language models together]{.tag} The pipelines of ch. 12 raise several open problems: building reliable knowledge graphs from text with LLMs, retrieving the right subgraph for a question (He and coauthors, 2024), evaluating global, corpus-level answers (Edge and coauthors, 2024), and giving LLMs a faithful view of graph structure, through verbalisation or message-passing encoders. A unifying roadmap is proposed by Pan and coauthors (2024).
:::

::: note
[Remark 14.7 — Extreme compression]{.tag} Below 4 bits, round-to-nearest collapses and methods rely on incoherence processing, vector quantization or quantization-aware training; QuIP (Chee and coauthors, 2023) obtains 2-bit weights with guarantees under an incoherence assumption. How quantization interacts with scaling laws, long contexts (quantized KV caches) and fine-tuning (QLoRA) is an active area.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 14

-   Graph-of-words ideas live on in summarisation, neural classifiers and, potentially, retrieval.
-   Efficient attention and state-space models attack the quadratic cost; length extrapolation remains open.
-   Preference optimisation, verifiable rewards and evaluation methodology are moving fast and lack theory.
-   Multilingual fairness, graph–LLM integration and sub-4-bit compression are open engineering and research fronts.
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

Levels: ★ apply the course, ★★ combine or prove a short result, ★★★ open-ended or research-flavoured. The *Practice* column of the [session plan](#sessions) says when to do each one.

1.  **★ TF-IDF, cosine and perplexity by hand.** Three documents: $d_1$ = “graph graph kernel”, $d_2$ = “graph words”, $d_3$ = “words vectors”.

    (a) Compute the TF-IDF vectors with natural logarithms and $N = 3$. (b) Compute the cosine of $d_1$ with $d_2$ and with $d_3$. (c) A model gives probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 and 0.125 to the four tokens of a test sentence; what is its perplexity?

    *Solution*: (a) “graph” has $\mathrm{df} = 2$ and “kernel” $\mathrm{df} = 1$, so $d_1$ has weights $2 \log 1.5 = 0.811$ and $\log 3 = 1.099$.

    The document $d_2$ has $\log 1.5 = 0.405$ for “graph” and for “words”; $d_3$ has 1.099 for “vectors” and 0.405 for “words”.

    (b) The norms are 1.366 and 0.573, and only “graph” is shared, so
    $$
    \cos(d_1, d_2) = \frac{0.811 \times 0.405}{1.366 \times 0.573} \approx 0.42, \qquad \cos(d_1, d_3) = 0.
    $$

    (c) The product of the probabilities is $1/512$, so the perplexity is $512^{1/4} = 2^{9/4} \approx 4.76$.

2.  **★ BPE by hand.** Run four BPE merges on the word counts “low” 5, “lowest” 2, “newer” 6, “wider” 3, “new” 2 (break ties by first occurrence). Segment “lower” and “newest” with the learned merges, and check with the code of Example 1.10.

    *Solution*: the initial pair counts are 9 for “e r”, 8 for “w e”, “n e” and “e w”, and 7 for “l o” and “o w”. The merges are “er” (9), “ne” (8), “new” (8) and “lo” (7); after “er”, the pair “w e” only remains in “lowest” (count 2).

    “lower” becomes “lo w er” and “newest” becomes “new e s t”. The code prints the merges `[('er', 9), ('ne', 8), ('new', 8), ('lo', 7)]`.

3.  **★ Cores by hand.** A graph-of-words has the edges A–B, A–C, B–C, A–D, B–D and D–E. Run the peeling algorithm of Theorem 3.3, give every core number, the degeneracy, the main core and the CoreRank scores.

    *Solution*: remove E (degree 1, so $\kappa = 1$); then C and D have degree 2. Remove C ($\kappa = 2$), then D (degree 2), then A and B (degrees 1 and 0, $\kappa$ stays 2).

    Core numbers: E 1, and A, B, C, D 2. The degeneracy is 2 and the main core is $\{A, B, C, D\}$. CoreRank: A 6, B 6, D 5, C 4, E 2, which orders the terms of the main core.

4.  **★ Additive, dot and scaled attention.** Take the data of Example 4.8.

    Compute the weights and the context for additive attention with $W_a = U_a = I$ and $v = (1, 1)$, and for scaled dot-product attention with $d_k = 2$. Compare with Example 4.8.

    *Solution*: additive scores $v^\top \tanh(s + h_j)$ are 1.726, 1.523 and 0.995, so the weights are $(0.435, 0.355, 0.210)$ and the context is $(0.854, 0.790)$.

    Scaled scores are $(0.707, 0, 1.414)$, with weights $(0.284, 0.140, 0.576)$ and context $(1.436, 0.424)$.

    The additive score ranks $h_1$ first: the tanh saturates the large coordinate of $s + h_3$, so it rewards keys active in both coordinates. The $\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling keeps the ranking of Example 4.8 and only softens it (0.576 instead of 0.665 on $h_3$).

5.  **★ LoRA and KV-cache budgets.** A decoder has 32 layers, model width 4096 and heads of dimension 128. (a) How many parameters does LoRA of rank 16 on $W_Q$ and $W_V$ of every layer train, and how many megabytes do they take in 16 bits? (b) What is the KV-cache memory for a batch of 8 sequences of 2048 tokens in 16 bits, with 32 key–value heads, and with grouped-query attention using 8?

    *Solution*: (a) Each matrix gets $16 \times (4096 + 4096) = 131{,}072$ parameters, so $2 \times 32 \times 131{,}072 \approx 8.4$ million in total, about 16.8 MB (Proposition 10.3).

    (b) By Proposition 13.7, $2 \times 32 \times 32 \times 128 \times 2048 \times 8 \times 2$ bytes $= 8$ GiB with 32 heads, and 2 GiB with 8 key–value heads.

6.  **★ A compute budget.** You may spend $10^{22}$ operations. (a) With the rule of 20 tokens per parameter and $C = 6ND$, what model size and how many tokens? (b) How long does training take on 256 accelerators sustaining $4 \times 10^{14}$ operations per second each? (c) Using the code of Example 8.6, what does the fitted law of Theorem 8.4 recommend instead?

    *Solution*: (a) $C = 6 N \cdot 20 N = 120 N^2$, so $N \approx 9.1 \times 10^9$ parameters and $D \approx 1.8 \times 10^{11}$ tokens. (b) The 256 accelerators deliver about $10^{17}$ operations per second, so training takes about $9.8 \times 10^4$ seconds, a little more than a day.

    (c) The fitted law gives a smaller model trained on more tokens (a ratio of about 60 tokens per parameter at this budget): the two estimation methods disagree, which is why Example 8.6 discusses the replication.

7.  **★★ SGNS with a smoothed noise law.** Redo the proof of Theorem 2.4 with negatives drawn from $P_n(c) = \#(c)^{3/4} / Z$. Show that the optimum is a PMI computed with a smoothed context distribution, shifted by $\log k$. Explain why rare contexts get smaller PMI values than with the unigram law, and what a finite dimension changes.

    *Solution*: the term of the pair $(w, c)$ becomes
    $$
    f(x) = \#(w, c) \log \sigma(x) + k\, \#(w)\, P_n(c) \log \sigma(-x),
    $$
    concave in $x$, with maximum at
    $$
    x^* = \log \frac{\#(w, c)}{\#(w)\, P_n(c)} - \log k.
    $$
    Raising counts to the power $3/4$ increases the probability of rare contexts, which lowers their PMI and damps the known bias of PMI towards rare pairs.

    With a finite dimension, the inner products cannot reach all the targets: SGNS then computes a weighted low-rank approximation, with weights given by the counts, unlike the unweighted SVD of Proposition 2.5.

8.  **★★ Max pooling, exclusive or, and order (computational).** (a) Show that a width-1 convolution with max pooling and a linear output can represent the label of Example 1.4: positive when exactly one of “not” and “good” occurs. (b) Run Example 5.5 with `width=1`. (c) Change the generator so that the core is “good bad” (label 1) or “bad good” (label 0), and compare widths 1 and 2.

    *Solution*: (a) With one-hot vectors, a filter that responds 1 to “not” and to “good” gives, after max pooling, the *or* of the two presences $A$ and $B$; two more filters give $A$ and $B$. The output $2\,\mathrm{OR} - A - B$ equals the exclusive or.

    (b) The width-1 network also reaches 1.000: the task depends only on which words occur, and the non-linearity of max pooling suffices. (c) Both classes now have the same bag of words: width 1 stays at chance (0.458 in our run), width 2 reaches 1.000.

9.  **★★ Positions: sinusoids versus rotations.** (a) Show that, for each frequency, the pair $(\sin, \cos)$ of Definition 6.6 at position $p + k$ is the pair at $p$ rotated by the angle $k \omega_i$.

    (b) For $d_k = 2$, write the RoPE score of Theorem 6.8 with the angles $\varphi_q$, $\varphi_k$ of $q$ and $k$. (c) Show that adding sinusoidal codes to the inputs does not make attention scores depend on the offset only.

    *Solution*: (a) The addition formulas give
    $$
    \sin((p + k)\omega) = \sin(p\omega)\cos(k\omega) + \cos(p\omega)\sin(k\omega),
    $$
    and similarly for the cosine: a rotation matrix that does not depend on $p$.

    (b) The score is
    $$
    \|q\|\, \|k\| \cos\big(\varphi_k - \varphi_q + (n - m)\theta\big).
    $$
    For $q = k = (1, 0)$, $\theta = \pi/6$, $m = 1$ and $n = 3$, it is $\cos(\pi/3) = 0.5$.

    (c) With $x_m + p_m$ as input, the score $(x_m + p_m)^\top W_Q^\top W_K (x_n + p_n)$ contains the cross terms $x_m^\top W_Q^\top W_K\, p_n$, which depend on the absolute position $n$.

10. **★★ Pretraining objectives compared.** (a) How many supervised predictions does a 512-token sequence give under masked language modelling with a 15 % rate, and under causal language modelling? (b) Why can a decoder generate with a cache of past keys and values, while a bidirectional encoder must recompute everything when a token is appended? (c) Why does BART text infilling sometimes insert a mask that hides zero tokens?

    *Solution*: (a) About $0.15 \times 512 \approx 77$ predictions against 511: causal pretraining extracts more signal per token, one reason why it dominates at scale.

    (b) Under the causal mask, the states of past positions do not depend on later tokens, so they can be cached and reused. In an encoder, every state depends on every token, so appending one changes all of them.

    (c) Since a mask may hide zero, one or several tokens, the model must predict the length of each span, not only its content; this prepares it for generation of variable-length text.

11. **★★ Metrics and distillation (computational).** (a) Compute $\mathrm{BLEU}_2$ of “the cat sits on the mat” against “the cat is on the mat”. (b) Prove the gradient formula of Proposition 9.5. (c) Run Example 9.7 with student dimensions $k = 2, 4, 8, 16$ and plot Kendall's tau against $k$.

    *Solution*: (a) As in Example 9.2, $p_1 = 5/6$ and $p_2 = 3/5$, so $\mathrm{BLEU}_2 \approx 0.707$: the near-synonym is treated as an error.

    (b) The KL term equals a cross-entropy with soft targets $p$ minus a constant; by Proposition 0.2 applied to the logits $z^S / \tau$, its gradient in $z^S$ is $(q - p)/\tau$.

    (c) With the seeds of the example, tau is 0.28, 0.51, 0.72 and 0.86 for $k = 2, 4, 8, 16$. The unigram F1 (0.40) is beaten from $k = 4$ on: a small learned model captures the synonym structure that exact matching misses.

12. **★★ DPO at initialisation and in the deterministic limit.** (a) Show that adding any function $f(x)$ to the reward changes neither $\pi^*$ nor the preference probabilities. (b) At $\pi_\theta = \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$, give the value of the DPO loss and its gradient. (c) In Example 11.8, suppose the better answer always wins. What happens to the DPO solution?

    *Solution*: (a) $\exp(f(x)/\beta)$ cancels in the normalisation of Theorem 11.3, and $f(x)$ cancels in the reward difference of Definition 11.1.

    (b) The margin is 0, the loss is $\log 2 \approx 0.693$, and every pair weighs the same in the gradient:
    $$
    \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}} = -\frac{\beta}{2}\, \mathbb{E}\big[\nabla \log \pi_\theta(y_w) - \nabla \log \pi_\theta(y_l)\big].
    $$

    (c) The Bradley–Terry likelihood is then maximised only by infinite reward gaps, so the logits diverge and the policy collapses on the best answer, whatever $\beta$. The KL regularisation is lost; this overfitting motivates the IPO variant of Azar and coauthors (2024).

13. **★★ Quantization error and outliers (computational).** Draw 4096 weights from a standard normal law, set the first one to 20, and quantize on 4 bits with absmax scales per tensor, per group of 128 and per group of 32. Compare the mean squared error with the prediction $s^2/12$ of Proposition 13.2, and give the storage cost in bits per weight.

    *Solution*: with `numpy.random.default_rng(0)`, the errors are 0.612, 0.034 and 0.013, against mean predictions 0.680, 0.034 and 0.015; the costs are 4.004, 4.125 and 4.5 bits per weight.

    Per tensor, the step is $20/7 \approx 2.9$, so almost every weight rounds to zero and the error is close to the variance of the weights. The prediction fails there because errors are not uniform when the step exceeds the spread of the data.

14. **★★★ The shortest-path kernel for documents.** Implement Definition 3.7 with windows of 3 and $d_{\max} = 2$, compute the normalised Gram matrix of “the cat sat on the mat”, “on the mat the cat sat” and “the dog chased the cat”, check its eigenvalues, and discuss the cost and the roles of the window and of $d_{\max}$.

    *Hints and expected result*: one implementation uses breadth-first search from every node, as below.

    ```python
    import numpy as np, networkx as nx
    from collections import Counter

    def gow(text, window=3):
        t = text.lower().split()
        G = nx.Graph(); G.add_nodes_from(t)
        G.add_edges_from((t[i], u) for i in range(len(t)) for u in t[i + 1:i + window] if u != t[i])
        return G

    def sp_features(G, d_max=2):
        phi = Counter()
        for a, dist in nx.all_pairs_shortest_path_length(G, cutoff=d_max):
            for b, l in dist.items():
                if a < b:
                    phi[a, b, l] += 1
        return phi

    def sp_kernel(G1, G2):
        f1, f2 = sp_features(G1), sp_features(G2)
        k = lambda f, g: sum(v * g[key] for key, v in f.items())
        return k(f1, f2) / np.sqrt(k(f1, f1) * k(f2, f2))

    docs = ["the cat sat on the mat", "on the mat the cat sat", "the dog chased the cat"]
    G = [gow(d) for d in docs]
    K = np.array([[sp_kernel(a, b) for b in G] for a in G])
    print(np.round(K, 3), np.round(np.linalg.eigvalsh(K), 3))
    ```

    The off-diagonal values are 0.700 for the two permuted sentences and 0.129 for the third. The eigenvalues 0.300, 0.955 and 1.745 are non-negative, as Proposition 3.8 guarantees.

    Breadth-first search from every node costs $O(n(n + m))$ per document. A larger window adds edges and shortens distances; a larger $d_{\max}$ adds features and makes the kernel closer to a bag of term pairs.

15. **★★★ A multi-hop retrieval benchmark.** Generate a synthetic knowledge graph of about 200 entities and 5 relations, turn every triple into a one-sentence passage, and generate two-hop questions whose answer needs two triples. Compare BM25 over passages (Definition 12.1) with entity linking plus $k$-hop expansion (Example 12.7), by recall at $k$ of the two supporting passages.

    *Hints and expected result*: BM25 retrieves the first-hop passage, which shares the entity name with the question, but rarely the second, which shares no word with it. Graph expansion retrieves both when entity linking succeeds, at the price of many distractors when nodes have high degree.

    A good report shows recall at $k$ against $k$ for both methods, and a hybrid — BM25 for the first hop, the graph for the next — that combines their strengths. This is the motivation of the pipelines of Definition 12.6.

16. **★★★ Tokenizer fertility across languages.** Build two synthetic languages with different syllable inventories and word-length distributions, train BPE (Example 1.10) on a mixture that contains 90 % of language A, and measure the fertility (Definition 8.7) on each language. Vary the mixture and the vocabulary size, and relate the results to Petrov and coauthors (2023).

    *Hints and expected result*: fertility on the minority language is clearly higher, and the gap shrinks as its share or the vocabulary size grows. Express the cost of a fixed text in tokens and in context-window usage for both languages, and discuss what a sovereign model gains by training its own tokenizer (Remark 9.10).

## Projects and assessment {#projects}

The official assessment (master-mva.com) is a final data challenge plus a lab-based evaluation; the Université Paris-Saclay course detail describes it as non-integral continuous assessment (“Evaluation Continue non Intégrale”). No weights and no written exam are displayed. The group subjects below are shaped like a data challenge, the solo subjects are paper studies and lab extensions, and the written exam is only a self-assessment proposal.

### Solo projects {#projects-solo}

1.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] Paper study: keyword extraction by graph degeneracy (Rousseau and Vazirgiannis, 2015; Tixier, Malliaros and Vazirgiannis, 2016).** Question: do main-core retention and CoreRank beat TF-IDF and TextRank (Mihalcea and Tarau, 2004) on single-document keyword extraction?
    -   Implement the weighted graph-of-words, main-core retention, CoreRank with a rule for the number of keywords, TextRank (PageRank on the same graph) and a TF-IDF baseline (ch. 1, 3).
    -   Evaluate precision, recall and F1 with stemmed exact matching on the public abstracts of Hulth (2003) or the SemEval-2010 keyphrase data (Kim and coauthors, 2010), with an ablation on the window size.
    -   Deliverables: code, a 4–6 page report, a 10-minute talk. Success: the paper's ranking of the methods is reproduced or its failure explained.

2.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] Paper study: DPO against reward modelling and policy gradient (Rafailov and coauthors, 2023).** Question: on a controlled problem with a known reward, when do the two routes reach the same policy?
    -   Extend Example 11.8 to many prompts with a tabular policy. Implement reward-model fitting followed by KL-regularised policy gradient, DPO, and the IPO variant (Azar and coauthors, 2024).
    -   Plot reward against KL divergence from the reference, sample efficiency, and the effect of nearly deterministic preferences (Exercise 12). Chapters 0, 11.
    -   Deliverables: code, a 4–6 page report, a 10-minute talk. Success: both routes reach the same frontier on Bradley–Terry data, and the degeneration of DPO on deterministic preferences is shown and corrected.

3.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] How low can rank and bits go?** Question: what LoRA rank and how many bits does a small open model need on a classification task?
    -   Fine-tune GPT-2 small (124 million parameters, public weights) with LoRA of rank 1 to 64 on SST-2 (Socher and coauthors, 2013), on a free GPU tier (ch. 10).
    -   Merge the adapters, quantize the model with round-to-nearest and the GPTQ procedure of Example 13.8 at 8, 4 and 3 bits, and report accuracy and WikiText-2 perplexity (Merity and coauthors, 2017) (ch. 13).
    -   Deliverables: code, a 4–6 page report, a 10-minute talk. Success: an accuracy-versus-rank curve with a clear knee, and GPTQ at least as good as round-to-nearest at 4 and 3 bits.

### Group projects {#projects-group}

1.  **[Group of 2–3 · ≈ 30 h each] Data challenge: classifying papers from their text and their citations.** Use the ogbn-arxiv citation graph of the Open Graph Benchmark (Hu and coauthors, 2020) with the public titles and abstracts of its papers; the task is the subject area, on the official split.
    -   Member 1: text models — TF-IDF with logistic regression, then a small pretrained encoder, frozen or fine-tuned with LoRA (ch. 1, 7, 10).
    -   Member 2: graph models — label propagation and message passing over citations (Definition 12.6), with graph-of-words features (ch. 3).
    -   Member 3: fusion, hidden test set, leaderboard and error analysis.
    -   Deliverables: code, a 6–8 page report, a 15-minute talk. Success: the fused model beats the group's best text-only and best graph-only models on the hidden split, with ablations.

2.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 30 h each] A grounded, graph-augmented question-answering system.** Use the distractor setting of HotpotQA (Yang and coauthors, 2018), whose questions need two supporting paragraphs.
    -   Retrieval: BM25 and a small public dense encoder, evaluated by recall at $k$ of the supporting paragraphs (ch. 12).
    -   Graph: an entity graph built from the paragraphs, with $k$-hop expansion from the entities of the question (Example 12.7).
    -   Generation: a small open instruction-tuned model, or an extractive reader, prompted to cite paragraphs; exact match, F1 and citation correctness (ch. 9, 12).
    -   Deliverables: code, a 6–8 page report, a 15-minute talk. Success: graph expansion raises supporting-paragraph recall on bridge questions over BM25 alone, and the answer metrics follow.

3.  **[Group of 2–3 · ≈ 30 h each] Paper study: distilling an evaluation metric (Kamal Eddine and coauthors, 2022).** Reproduce FrugalScore at small scale.
    -   Member 1: generate candidate–reference pairs from a public summarisation corpus such as CNN/DailyMail (Hermann and coauthors, 2015) and score them with BERTScore (Zhang and coauthors, 2020) as teacher.
    -   Member 2: train compact pretrained students (Turc and coauthors, 2019) to regress the teacher scores (Proposition 9.5, Example 9.7).
    -   Member 3: meta-evaluation against the human judgements of SummEval (Fabbri and coauthors, 2021), and speed benchmarks.
    -   Deliverables: code, a 6–8 page report, a 15-minute talk. Success: the student keeps most of the teacher's Kendall correlation with human judgements while running at least ten times faster.

### Written exam (proposal) {#projects-exam}

Format: 2 hours, one handwritten A4 sheet allowed, no electronic device, four questions.

1.  **Question (4 points).** Define the $k$-core of a graph, the core number of a node and the degeneracy. Describe main-core keyword extraction on a graph-of-words, explain why it needs no corpus statistics, unlike TF-IDF, and give one limitation.

    *Expected*: Definitions 3.1–3.2 and the peeling algorithm of Theorem 3.3; the score uses only the document's own graph (Definition 3.4). Limitations: on short texts the main core is coarse, which CoreRank refines; the result depends on the window size and on preprocessing.

2.  **Question (5 points).** (a) Under the rule of 20 tokens per parameter, how many tokens and operations does a model of $10^9$ parameters need? (b) How many parameters does LoRA of rank 8 add to a $2048 \times 2048$ matrix? (c) What is the KV-cache memory of one sequence of 4096 tokens for 24 layers, 16 key–value heads of dimension 128, in 16 bits?

    *Expected*: (a) $D = 2 \times 10^{10}$ tokens and $C = 6ND = 1.2 \times 10^{20}$ operations. (b) $8 \times (2048 + 2048) = 32{,}768$ parameters, 0.78 % of the matrix. (c) By Proposition 13.7, $2 \times 24 \times 16 \times 128 \times 4096 \times 2$ bytes, that is 768 MiB.

3.  **Question (5 points).** One query attends to three keys with $d_k = 2$:
    $$
    q = (1, 0); \quad k_1 = (1, 0),\ k_2 = (0, 1),\ k_3 = (-1, 0); \quad v_1 = (1, 0),\ v_2 = (0, 1),\ v_3 = (1, 1).
    $$
    Compute the attention weights and the output. Then apply a causal mask, the query being at position 2, and recompute. Finally, explain why self-attention without positions cannot distinguish “good bad” from “bad good”.

    *Expected*: scaled scores $(0.707, 0, -0.707)$, weights $(0.576, 0.284, 0.140)$, output $(0.716, 0.424)$. With the mask only $k_1, k_2$ remain: weights $(0.670, 0.330)$ and output $(0.670, 0.330)$. Without positions, self-attention is permutation-equivariant (Proposition 6.4), so any pooled output is the same for both orders.

4.  **Question (6 points).** For a reward $r$, a reference policy and $\beta > 0$, prove that the maximiser of the KL-regularized objective is the reference tilted by $\exp(r/\beta)$. Deduce the DPO loss under the Bradley–Terry model, and explain what happens when the policy equals the reference.

    *Expected*: the Gibbs argument of Theorem 11.3, writing the objective as $-\beta\, \mathrm{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \pi^*) + \beta \log Z$; inversion of the optimal policy and cancellation of $\log Z(x)$ in the reward difference (Theorem 11.6). At the reference, the margin is 0 and the loss is $\log 2$ (Exercise 12).

### Grading rubric (proposal) {#projects-rubric}

| Criterion | Weight | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Correctness and rigour | 25 % | methods implemented as defined in the chapters; derivations checked; no data leakage between training and evaluation |
| Experimental protocol | 20 % | honest baselines (TF-IDF, BM25, round-to-nearest), held-out data, fixed seeds, error bars (Proposition 9.9) |
| Results and analysis | 20 % | the success criterion is met or its failure explained; ablations and error analysis |
| Code and reproducibility | 15 % | a script or notebook that reruns every number of the report from public data |
| Written report | 10 % | clear question, related work with real references, figures that make the point |
| Talk and questions | 10 % | the main result in ten minutes; precise answers on the methods |
